performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: John Harrison and the Wichita State University Chamber Players play the first movement, Allegro, of Spring, RV 269, from The Four Seasons. In it three violins imitate birds, running semiquavers represent water, and a storm interrupts the sunshine, and the score names what each of these spring sounds stands for.

sections.label: A · Opening refrain, E major
sections.mNote: Full strings announce E major, then echo themselves softly.

sections.label: B · Three violins with trills
sections.mNote: Trills and calls in turn above E and B.

sections.label: A′ · Refrain and stream episode
sections.mNote: The refrain’s second phrase returns, followed by the stream episode.

sections.label: C · Thunder and lightning
sections.mNote: Repeated notes and violin arpeggios lead to C♯ minor.

sections.label: A″ · Refrain in E major
sections.mNote: The bass descends through C♯, F♯, B and E.

sections.label: A′ · E major, closing phrase and echo
sections.mNote: The closing phrase returns, followed by its soft echo.

relations.label: The ritornello closes the movement
relations.basis: The closing orchestral ritornello recalls the later phrases of the E-major opening refrain. The measured pair agrees with the closing section near 194 s; it does not imply that every bar of the first ritornello returns. CENS diagonal mean 0.965, sustained 14.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 175.5 s (cache/form/vivaldi-spring-allegro.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening in E major
cues.text: The 1725 sonnet begins: “Giunt’é la Primavera e festosetti / La Salutan gl’Augei con lieto canto” — “Spring has arrived, and the birds joyfully greet her with happy song.” The strings establish E major in firm phrases, each followed by a soft echo.
cues.evidence: Sonnet accompanying Vivaldi’s Op. 8 (1725), letters A–B; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 1–13: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301. The poems were published anonymously.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Spring at the Concert Spirituel, Paris
cues.text: Spring was the work played on eleven of the sixteen Vivaldi occasions at the Concert Spirituel in Paris between 1736 and 1763. Michel Corrette turned it into a motet in 1765, and Rousseau made it into a piece for solo flute in 1775.
cues.evidence: Paul Everett, Vivaldi: The Four Seasons and Other Concertos, Op. 8 (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1996), on the Seasons in Paris: Spring on eleven of sixteen Vivaldi occasions at the Concert Spirituel, 1736–63; Corrette’s motet Laudate Dominum de coelis (1765); Rousseau’s version for unaccompanied flute (1775). Martin Pearlman’s Boston Baroque note names the same Concert Spirituel performances and both arrangements. https://baroque.boston/vivaldi-four-seasons

cues.title: The streams, bars 31–40
cues.text: “E i fonti allo Spirar de’ Zeffiretti / Con dolce mormorio Scorrono intanto” — “Meanwhile the streams flow with a sweet murmur beneath the little breezes.” The violins play the streams of the sonnet in semiquavers. Repeated bass notes hold the passage in E major.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter C; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 31–40; José Rodríguez Alvira’s score commentary uses this recording: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Storm episode, bars 44–59
cues.text: “Vengon’ coprendo l’aer di nero amanto / E Lampi, e tuoni ad annuntiarla eletti” — “Lightning and thunder come, chosen to announce her, covering the sky with a black cloak.” Vivaldi set the storm as repeated notes beneath racing arpeggios from the solo violin. The music reaches C♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter D; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 44–59, and Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the birds, C♯ minor
cues.text: “Indi tacendo questi, gl’Augelletti / Tornan’ di nuovo al lor canoro incanto” — “Then, when these fall silent, the little birds return to their enchanting song.” In bars 59–65 the trills return in C♯ minor. The continuo holds a long C♯ underneath them, where the bass was silent earlier.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter E; translation ours. Mutopia score, I, bars 59–65, including the sustained continuo C♯: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final ritornello and piano echo
cues.text: The full strings play the closing phrase of the ritornello in E major. Vivaldi repeats it piano, and the movement ends with B moving to E in the bass.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, I, closing tutti and piano echo, bars 76–82. Rodríguez Alvira identifies the final shortened ritornello: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Three violin parts after the cadence
transitions.how: The bass resolves from B to E, and then the bass and violas stop. Three violin parts continue: the soloist and two orchestral violins exchange trills and short calls. Held notes on E and B in the violins keep the birdsong in E major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, I, bars 13–27: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: Bass returns on E for the refrain
transitions.how: The bass returns on E, and the strings play the refrain’s second phrase together. A major chords pass over the repeated E before B resolves to E at the cadence. The next stream stays in the same key, with paired violin semiquavers above repeated bass quavers.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 27–40; harmony shown in Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.

transitions.title: Thunder on the bass B
transitions.how: The refrain reaches B major. Its bass B becomes a barrage of repeated demisemiquavers, marked thunder, and the solo violin follows with rapid arpeggios. The storm moves through E major towards C♯ minor, where the refrain’s closing phrase returns.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 40–59, including Tuoni in the bass; key sequence in Rodríguez Alvira’s commentary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.

transitions.title: Bass line returning to E major
transitions.how: After the bird calls the strings play together again. Beneath the refrain the bass moves C♯–F♯–B–E, giving C♯ minor, F♯ minor seventh, B seventh and E major. F♯ minor seventh belongs to both keys and serves as the pivot back to E major, the key of the concerto’s opening.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, bars 66–70; the progression is shown in Rodríguez Alvira’s score example: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php.

transitions.title: The tutti returns with the closing phrase
transitions.to: A′ · E major, closing phrase and echo
transitions.how: The last solo ends over E and B in the bass. The tutti resumes on E with the refrain’s closing phrase, then repeats it piano. The bass closes with a B–E cadence in the home key, and the Allegro tempo continues unchanged to the last chord.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, I, final solo and tutti, bars 70–82: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

source.title: Vivaldi, Spring, RV 269, full score (Mutopia, after Performers’ Facsimiles)
source.locator: I. Allegro, bars 1–82; spring1.ly and spring1a–f.ly. Continuo is represented by the bowed basses; its keyboard realisation is not specified.

timeline.note: Soloist and first violins share the refrain above repeated bass notes.
Three violin lines exchange bird calls; violas and the continuo bass rest.
The bass rejoins the refrain; paired violins then play semiquavers in the stream episode.
Repeated string notes alternate with the soloist’s rapid storm arpeggios.
Bird calls return over a held C♯ bass; violas rest.
The strings together play the refrain, moving from C♯ minor towards E major.
The solo violin decorates the held bass while the other upper strings rest.
All strings play the refrain’s closing phrase again, followed by its quieter echo.

composer.epithet: Venetian composer of concertos for the women of the Pietà and operas for the city’s theatres, who wrote a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 Antonio Vivaldi, a twenty-five-year-old Venetian, was ordained priest in March and became a violin teacher in September. He had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and went on helping with his career long after the son had become famous. In Venice Antonio was known as il prete rosso, the red priest. He worked in the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year. In 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 they took him back.
